analysis.one_liner: Terminates the federal income tax code and requires Congress to approve a replacement tax system by a set deadline.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013, despite 53 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end every federal tax imposed under the Internal Revenue Code — income, corporate, and estate taxes — after 2015, keeping only payroll taxes like Social Security and Medicare. Congress would be required to approve a replacement system by July 4, 2015, and delaying the termination would take a two-thirds vote in each chamber. The bill lists principles the new system should follow — a low rate for everyone, no tax bias against savings and investment — but contains no actual replacement plan. It sat in committee without a hearing until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and investors, if the replacement followed the bill's stated principles of a low flat rate and eliminating taxes on savings and investment income. Corporations and large estates would also stop paying income, corporate, and estate taxes under the termination provision.

how_it_helps.text: Ends every federal tax imposed under the Internal Revenue Code after 2015 — including income, corporate, and estate taxes — while preserving only self-employment, Social Security and Medicare payroll, and railroad retirement taxes.
Declares that any replacement system should apply a low rate to all Americans, eliminate the tax bias against savings and investment, and provide relief for working Americans.
Requires Congress to approve the new tax system in final form by July 4, 2015, and makes delaying the termination date require a two-thirds vote of Members in each chamber.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and consumers, who would keep paying payroll taxes on wages and would likely bear more of the burden under a replacement that taxes spending and wages rather than investment income. If Congress missed its own deadline, the federal government would lose most of its revenue, threatening funding for programs ordinary people rely on.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners and federal program beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: The bill terminates all income, corporate, and estate taxes with no guaranteed replacement; if Congress failed to approve a new system by the July 4, 2015 deadline, the federal government would lose most of its funding for everything from the military to Medicare benefits beyond payroll taxes.

The bill's stated principles — a low rate for all Americans and no tax bias against savings and investment — describe a flat or consumption-based tax, which would cut taxes most for households with large investment income and shift the burden toward wages and everyday spending.
The bill contains no actual replacement plan, only a list of principles, so taxpayers would be asked to end the current tax code without knowing what would take its place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A simpler tax code could genuinely reduce the cost and hassle of filing for ordinary families, and the bill's supporters framed it as protecting taxpayers from an overly complex code. But the bill sets no actual replacement system, and its declared principles point toward a tax structure that favors investment income over wages. It also carried a real risk: terminate the code, miss the deadline, and the government loses most of its revenue. As written, the benefit to ordinary taxpayers is speculative while the risks are concrete.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in January 2011, which never held a hearing or brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Goodlatte introduced the Tax Code Termination Act on January 26, 2011, with 41 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Rules Committee; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
It attracted 53 cosponsors — 52 Republicans and 1 Democrat — but that support never translated into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing tax code stayed in place. High-income households and investors continued paying taxes on savings and investment income, while ordinary taxpayers avoided being handed an untested replacement that contained no actual plan beyond a list of principles.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no one moved it forward

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors across the House.

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican — 52 of the 53 cosponsors were Republicans, with a single Democrat — and the bill received no committee or floor action.

industries.note: The bill ends taxes on investment income and directs that the replacement system 'eliminate the bias against savings and investment' with a low rate for everyone, which would cut taxes most for those with large capital income. The tax burden would shift toward wages and consumption, which is where most working families' income comes from.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Ending the Internal Revenue Code and replacing it with a simpler system would shrink the market for paid tax preparation and compliance services. That loss coincides with lower filing costs for ordinary taxpayers.

The bill explicitly preserves FICA and self-employment taxes, keeping the payroll tax system that funds Social Security and Medicare untouched. Workers and retirees would keep paying into and drawing from these programs as before.
